{{Short description|Theorem in computational complexity theory}}
'''Mahaney's theorem''' is a theorem in [[computational complexity theory]] proven by Stephen Mahaney that states that:

:If any [[sparse language]] is [[NP-complete|NP-hard]], then P = NP.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mahaney|first1=Stephen R.|title=Sparse complete sets for NP: Solution of a conjecture of Berman and Hartmanis|journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences|date=October 1982|volume=25|issue=2|pages=130–143|doi=10.1016/0022-0000(82)90002-2|hdl=1813/6257|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Note that the existence of an NP-hard sparse set implies the existence of an [[NP-complete]] sparse set.<ref>{{cite book |title=Structural Complexity II |last1=Balcázar |first1=José Luis |last2=Díaz |first2=Josep |last3=Gabarró |first3=Joaquim |year=1990 |isbn=3-540-52079-1 |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |pages=130–131}}</ref>

Mahaney's theorem was motivated by the [[Berman–Hartmanis conjecture]]:

:Given any two NP-complete sets <math>A, B</math>, there exists a pair of functions <math>f: A \to B, f^{-1}: B \to A</math> that are mutual inverses of each other, and are computable in polynomial time.

Since we know that some NP-complete sets are not sparse (for example, the set of satisfiable [[Boolean satisfiability problem|3SAT]] formulas), Berman and Hartmanis derived a second, weaker conjecture:

:There are no NP-complete sparse sets.

Mahaney's result shows that, if P ≠ NP, then indeed there are no NP-complete sparse sets, thus settling the second conjecture under the standard assumption of P ≠ NP.

The result was strengthened in 1991 to state that:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ogiwara |first=Mitsunori |last2=Watanabe |first2=Osamu |date=June 1991 |title=Polynomial-Time Bounded Truth-Table Reducibility of NP Sets to Sparse Sets |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0220030 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=471–483 |doi=10.1137/0220030 |issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

:If there exists a sparse language, such that a polynomial-time algorithm exists to solve the SAT problem by making O(1) queries to the sparse language [[Oracle machine|oracle]], then P = NP.

This is stronger than Mahaney's theorem, which is the special case where the polynomial-time algorithm can make at most 1 query to the sparse language protocol.
